Struggle stalwart, activist and towering figure in SA politics - we pay tribute to Winnie Madikizela-Mandela

Press Release:



Winnie Madikizela Mandela: uMkhonto weSizwe
In the years that Nelson Mandela languished in Robin Island, it was Winnie Madikizela-Mandela who took up the mantle, leading the struggle against apartheid from the front. A fearless leader, political activist and a towering figure in South Africa’s history – this is how millions of South Africans will continue to remember mam’ Winnie, who passed away earlier this week, after a long illness. As tributes pour in from around the world, Carte Blanche celebrates the life of an icon who was regarded as the “mother of the nation”.


Script:


Winnie Obit
Script 1
6 April 2018

Intro Sound Up Voices

Winnie: I’ve always known who the enemy of the people was throughout the years of my struggle.

Bantu Holomisa: Winnie was always in front of the battle, defending her own community.

Tokyo Sexwale: Winnie was no first lady, she was always a lady warrior.

Brigalia Bam: She fought for the rights of people, and contributed to the liberation of South Africa.

Winnie: It was a very traumatic kind of life. It bruises you inside, you bleed a lot…

Voice
This week South Africans received the news that 81 year old struggle stalwart Winnie Madikizela Mandela had passed away after a long illness.

Link Claire
Since hearing of her shocking passing on monday, people from far and wide have descended on Mam’ Winnie’s residence to pay their final respects. From ordinary citizens to the leadership of the governing party, they’ve all made their way here to her humble home.

Voice
Government has declared a period of mourning until her state funeral on the 14th of April, a fitting finale to a towering figure in our political history. But who was the woman that many called the mother of the nation.

Sound Up Tokyo
The mother of the nation - that’s not what she preferred. But to me and others, she was. And that nation is the nation of the unwashed.

Voice
Tokyo Sexwale is a man who needs little introduction. The former Premier of Gauteng and giant of the business world was a close personal friend of Winnie’s, who visited her just a few days before her passing.

Sound Up Tokyo
She could recognise and be a compatriot, a mother, a partner, to the poorest of the poor. Not just the poor, the poorest of the poor. These are people that people don’t even look at when they are passing with their Gucci shoes. But she’ll stop there, and they loved her.

Voice
Winnie was born in the former Transkei on the 26th of September 1936, in a rural village in Bizana. Long time friend and former leader of the homeland, Bantu Holomisa, says it provided Winnie with a solid foundation.

Sound Up Bantu Holomisa
The Transkei region, or area, was fortunate in that, right from time immemorial, education was high on the agenda of each and every household.




Sound Up Winnie Mandela
I was a countryside little girl, from the back-veldt of Pondoland. I hadn’t known anything from town life. I was straight from high school. And to me the cultural shock was traumatic.

Voice
A young Winnie first arrived in Johnnesburg in the early 1950’s, where she attended the Jan Hofmeyr school for Social Work . Fellow social worker and activist Doctor Brigalia Bam met Winnie at the school in 1955.

Sound Up Brigalia
She was very intellectual, very good student. Very keen on her work and education.

Voice
She was so good in fact that she soon landed a coveted job as a social worker at Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital in Soweto. It was here that she first experienced the devastating effects of the Apartheid regime.

Sound Up Brigalia
That becomes the biggest shock, when people tell you where they come from, how much they earn, their standard of living, the children don’t go to school. And that’s where Winnie began to see and realise life differently.

Sound Up Winnie
I could not imagine any human being subjecting a fellow human being to such inhumanity.

Voice
In 1954 she first met Nelson Mandela, who was a lawyer and already a prominent figure in the ANC. The couple married in 1958.

Sound Up Tokyo
When she married Madiba, who was 40 at that time, she was only 23. And married to this very powerful man, very very powerful. Very prominent in the African National Congress, a tough lawyer with Oliver Thambo, Tumba Nokwe and others, a social activist, a political activist, a boxer. So it is that world. She was thrust into this world, that vortex.

Sound Up Winnie
Our first date was to discuss finances of the organisation, which was in trouble then can you imagine. And we met to discuss raising funds for an organisation that didn’t have a cent in it’s name and they were faced with this mammoth trial, the treason trial.

Voice
The ANC was eventually banned, and by 1963 Winnie’s husband had been sent to Robben Island. Her campaign to free him, would change her life forever.

Link Claire
Winnie’s defiance of the state soon had her squarely in the sights of the Apartheid regime’s security forces. Her phone calls were monitored, she was surrounded by informants and she was at the centre of a plot to discredit the ANC.

Sound Up Bantu
On a daily basis they were harassed, on a daily basis they were shot at. Winnie was leading those units that were in the forefront.

Voice
As the pressure mounted, a defiant Winnie refused to lay down.


Sound Up Tokyo
Whilst Mandela is away, they would come, they would break the doors down. 8115 Villakazi street. They humiliated her, they dragged her. I lived there as a young man. She fought back and they slapped, they kicked, she fights. Winnie is a fighter. She falls and she stands up. You don’t want to see a woman fall like that.

Sound Up Brigalia
It was not Mandela who was telling Winnie go out and fight for people, the kinds of things Winnie was doing, there was no communication telling that woman what to do. There was no communication.

Voice
The ultimate torture came when Winnie was placed in solitary confinement at Pretoria Central Prison for 491 days.

Sound Up Winnie
You don’t know the difference between day and night. You don’t know what has happened to the children. You don’t know who else has been detained, you think you are alone in prison.

Sound Up Tokyo
People must never judge. You can’t judge until you are in the same position, where you are taken in the middle of the night, bleeding. These children, what do they do? They are so young. And she goes to detention.

Sound Up Winnie
It is in fact I think what shaped me. What brutalised me so much that I knew what it is to hate. For the first time I really discovered what the ruling class must be feeling against us.

Voice
For years, Madikizela-Mandela’s contribution to the struggle, has been marred by allegations that she was responsible for the death of 14-year old activist Stompie Seipei.

Sound Up Tokyo
Don’t talk, don’t judge, this candle in the wind, in the cross winds of South African politics. Don’t judge this brutality that she has gone through unless you are wearing that night dress which is torn…

Link Claire
Despite facing nearly daily brutality, Mam’ Winnie had the courage of her convictions. She could have fled the country at anytime, but instead chose to never leave her people.

Sound Up Tokyo
She sent many thousands of young people, men and women, abroad to be soldiers. She could have left with them. She didn’t. What a decision.

Sound Up Brigalia
Even at times when things were not easy, that woman would still pick up her bags and walk straight.

Voice
After nearly thirty years on the front lines of the struggle, Mam Winnie finally got to see her life’s work come to fruition with Madiba’s release in 1990.

Sound Up Release footage
There’s Mr Mandela, Mr Nelson Mandela, a free man taking his first steps into a new South Africa. Mrs Winnie Mandela next to him, waving to the crowds…

Sound Up Brigalia
If Winnie had sat quietly in her home, maybe Mandela would have also sat quietly and be not known by anybody. And to me I still think that is one of the most important things. It’s the preservation. Because without hope, you perish in that sort of arrangement.

Voice
Like all great leaders, Winnie Mandela was both a heroic and flawed individual. And while debates will continue about many of her decisions, no one can deny that she was a woman of incredible personal courage who will forever own her part in our country’s history.

Sound Up Winnie
I would either have been totally broken or survived, and I decided to survive.
